intuition: A cell can be reached from the cell above it or from the cell on its left. Add those two route counts to get the count for this cell. Save the counts as you move through the grid, so different routes do not make you solve the same smaller question repeatedly.

Every arrival comes from above or from the left. These groups cannot overlap because their final moves differ, so their counts add. Border cells have exactly one route: along the top row all moves are right, and along the left column all moves are down. These give the recurrence a concrete starting point.

The reference compresses the table into one row. Before updating a column, dp[col] still holds the previous row’s count from above. The neighboring dp[col-1] has already been updated and holds the current row’s count from the left. Adding them overwrites a value that is no longer needed.
The traversal order is therefore part of the algorithm, not merely a convenient loop arrangement.

Transposing the grid exchanges right and down moves in a one-to-one correspondence, so its number of paths is unchanged. The reference swaps dimensions when needed to retain the shorter DP row, reducing additional storage to O(min(m,n)).

steps: For m=3 and n=7, transpose the dimensions internally to seven rows and three columns, preserving the route count.
Initialize dp=[1,1,1] for the first row of the transposed grid.
The second row becomes [1,2,3]; the third becomes [1,3,6]. Each update combines the old above count with the updated left count.
Continue through rows four, five, and six: [1,4,10], [1,5,15], then [1,6,21].
The seventh row becomes [1,7,28]. Return its final count 28, which also counts all routes through the original 3-by-7 grid.

concept.question: How can route counts flow through a grid without listing the routes?
intuition: Listing all right-and-down routes repeats the same smaller path problem at many shared cells. We need only the number of routes reaching each cell.

Each arrival comes either from above or from the left. These two groups have different last moves, so their counts add without duplication. Process cells after their predecessor counts are known. A single remembered row is enough.
concept.observation: Add the above and left counts; neither group overlaps the other because their last moves differ.
approach: Give each top-row and left-column cell its one boundary route.
Add the two predecessor counts at each interior cell.
Read the count at the destination.
concept.correctness: A route to an interior cell has a unique final move, either right from the left cell or down from the above cell. Removing that move gives a route counted at its predecessor, and adding it reconstructs exactly one arrival route. The two groups are disjoint and complete, so adding their correct smaller counts gives the exact cell count.

complexity.explanation: Compute one count per cell, giving work proportional to the grid area. The reference remembers a row along the shorter dimension, so auxiliary memory grows only with that dimension.

pitfalls: Count routes, not just reachable cells.
Above and left counts must already be known.
A single-row grid still has one route.
